01_Why_the_table_has_groups_and_periods..title: Why the table has groups and periods
01_Why_the_table_has_groups_and_periods..subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe how the periodic table is arranged by increasing proton (atomic) number into periods and groups, and explain why elements in the same group show similar chemistry while metallic character generally decreases across a period.
Identify a trend in a set of supplied data for a group of elements and use it to make a cautious prediction about an unlisted element, distinguishing a general pattern from an exact rule.

prerequisites.statement: Electron configuration: the electrons of an atom are arranged in shells around the nucleus, and the number of electrons in the outermost (highest-numbered) shell can be read directly from the configuration, e.g. 2,8,1 for sodium.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Group chemistry is explained entirely by the number of outer-shell electrons, so a learner who cannot read off that number cannot connect a group's position to its shared chemistry.

prerequisites.statement: The periodic table is laid out as numbered rows (periods) and columns (groups), with a group number usually printed above each column.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Locating an element's period and group quickly, before reasoning about why it sits there, depends on recognising this layout convention.

diagnostic_items.question: Sodium has the electron arrangement 2,8,1. Lithium has 2,1. Both are in Group I. What do their arrangements have in common that explains this?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Both have exactly 1 electron in their outermost shell; it is this single outer electron, not the total number of electrons, that places them in the same group.

common_wrong_answers.answer: They both have the same total number of electrons.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner compares total electron count (3 for Li, 11 for Na) instead of isolating the outer shell, and concludes incorrectly that the two atoms have nothing numerical in common.

common_wrong_answers.answer: They are both metals, so they must be in the same group.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner uses a surface property (being a metal) as the explanation, skipping the electron-configuration reasoning that actually causes the group placement.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner isolates the outer-shell electron count as the defining similarity, rather than comparing total electron counts or surface appearance.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write both full configurations stacked with the outer shell circled in each, cover the inner shells with a hand or card, and ask the learner to compare only what remains visible.

theory_blocks.title: Same column, same chemistry?
theory_blocks.body:
Lithium, sodium and potassium are far from identical: they differ in softness, in melting point and in how violently they react when dropped into water.

Yet a chemist can predict, before testing, that all three will react with water to form a strongly alkaline solution and hydrogen gas.

The periodic table is built so that this kind of prediction works: elements are not arranged by appearance, or by when they were discovered,

but by a property of the atom itself that quietly controls its chemistry — [[blue:the number of electrons in its outermost shell]].

So the table answers two separate questions at once. Reading **down a column** (a group) tells you which elements are likely to behave alike.

Reading **along a row** (a period) tells you how character changes steadily as electrons are added, one at a time, to the same outer shell. Both axes come from the same underlying model of the atom; neither is arbitrary.

theory_blocks.title: Z fixes the order; outer electrons fix the groups
theory_blocks.body:
- The table is ordered by strictly **increasing proton number**, $Z$ (also called the atomic number): hydrogen is $Z=1$, helium $Z=2$, and so on with no gaps or exceptions.
- A **period** is a row. Moving along a period, atoms gain electrons into the *same* outer shell, one at a time; the number of occupied shells stays the same along the row.
- A **group** is a column. Elements in the same group have the *same number of electrons in their outermost shell*, which is why they tend to react in similar ways: chemistry is driven mainly by what happens to those outer electrons.
- Across a period, metallic character generally decreases from left to right: elements on the left (few outer electrons, easily lost) are metals, while elements on the right (nearly full outer shells) are non-metals.

The fragment below shows Periods 1 to 3, with the group numbering Cambridge uses: Groups I to VII for the main groups and Group VIII for the noble gases.

Group I and Group VII are highlighted: every highlighted element in a given column shares the same outer-electron count, while Period 2 and Period 3 each show character shifting steadily from metal to non-metal left to right.

Notice the gap between Group II and Group III in these rows — the block of transition metals that will fill it does not begin until Period 4, so there is nothing missing from this fragment, only a feature that appears later in the full table.

Hydrogen is drawn on its own above the table, as on the Cambridge data sheet: it has one outer electron, but it is not an alkali metal, so it is not placed in the Group I column.

Group I is highlighted in blue and Group VII in gold. Hydrogen is drawn on its own above the table, and the gap before Group III marks where the transition-metal block will appear from Period 4 onward.

theory_blocks.title: A period is not a group
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to assume that, because elements in the same group are alike, elements in the same period must also be alike in some matching way. They are not alike in the same sense.

Sodium (2,8,1) and chlorine (2,8,7) are both Period 3 elements: they have the same number of occupied shells (three), but their outer-shell electron counts are completely different (1 and 7),

and so is their chemistry — sodium is a soft, highly reactive metal, chlorine a reactive non-metal gas.

What a period guarantees is a shared [[blue:*number of shells*]]. What a group guarantees is a shared [[orange:*number of outer electrons*]].

Confusing the two leads to expecting a whole row to behave like a family, when it is really a whole column that does.

theory_blocks.title: Reading a trend without over-promising
theory_blocks.body:
Spotting a trend is a two-step skill: first describe what the data actually does, then decide how far you are entitled to extend it.

1. **Look at the whole sequence, not just two points.** A trend is a statement about the general direction across several data points, not a single jump.
2. **State the trend as 'generally increases/decreases', unless every single step genuinely agrees.** This leaves room for a real exception without the trend being wrong overall.
3. **A prediction beyond the supplied data is an estimate of a region, not an exact figure**, because the size of each step is not guaranteed to stay constant.

This matters because the syllabus expects predictions to be built from supplied data and expressed cautiously, not memorised as exact values. A trend that is 'generally true' is still extremely useful for prediction;

it is just not a guarantee for every individual case.

keywords.definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, written Z, which strictly fixes an element's position in the periodic table.
A row of the periodic table; its members share the same number of occupied electron shells.
A column of the periodic table; its members share the same number of outer-shell electrons and tend to show similar chemistry.
The highest-numbered electron shell that contains at least one electron in a given atom; its electron count determines group membership and most chemical behaviour.
The overall direction of change of a property across a group or period, which may still contain individual exceptions.

worked_examples.statement: **Locating magnesium.** Magnesium has proton number $Z=12$ and electron configuration 2,8,2. State its period and group, and justify each using the configuration.
solution: Three electron shells are occupied (2, then 8, then 2), so magnesium is in **Period 3**: the period number equals the number of occupied shells.
The outermost shell holds 2 electrons, so magnesium is in **Group II**: the group number (for Groups I to VII) equals the number of outer-shell electrons.
Both facts come from the same configuration, read in two different ways: count the shells for the period, read the last shell's total for the group.
worked_examples.interpretation: Locating an element from its configuration, rather than from memorising its position, is the skill that makes the period/group structure meaningful rather than arbitrary.

worked_examples.statement: **Same group, different totals.** A student says, 'sodium and potassium can't really be in the same group, because sodium has 11 electrons and potassium has 19 — that's not the same number at all.' Sodium's configuration is 2,8,1; potassium's is 2,8,8,1. Evaluate the student's claim.
solution: The student is comparing *total* electron counts (11 and 19), which are indeed different.
Group membership depends only on the *outer-shell* electron count, not the total: sodium's outer shell holds 1 electron, and potassium's outer shell also holds 1 electron.
Because both atoms have exactly one outer electron, despite very different totals, they belong to the same group (Group I) and share similar chemistry; the student's reasoning uses the wrong number.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Comparing total electron counts between elements instead of isolating the outermost shell before deciding on group membership.

worked_examples.statement: **Predicting with caution.** The boiling points of the noble gases helium, neon and argon are $-269\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $-246\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $-186\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ respectively. Using this trend, predict an approximate boiling point for krypton, the next noble gas down the group, and explain why your answer is an estimate rather than an exact value.
solution: List the step sizes: from He to Ne, the boiling point rises by $23\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($-269$ to $-246$); from Ne to Ar, it rises by $60\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($-246$ to $-186$).

The boiling point clearly rises down the group, and the size of the rise is itself increasing, so a reasonable estimate for krypton is somewhere noticeably higher than $-186\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, for example in the region of $-150\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $-100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

This is an estimate, not an exact figure, because the two known steps are not equal in size: nothing in the data guarantees the next step will match either of the previous two exactly. (Krypton's actual boiling point is $-153\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, inside this estimated region.)
worked_examples.interpretation: The point of the example is the reasoning about step sizes and the honest region-based answer, not the exact figure; this models the Supplement skill of predicting cautiously from supplied data.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the step size between the last two known values will repeat exactly, and giving a single precise number instead of a justified region.

guided_exercises.statement: Silicon has proton number $Z=14$ and electron configuration 2,8,4. State its period and group, and explain briefly why you would expect it to sit between a metal (aluminium, Group III) and a non-metal (phosphorus, Group V) in terms of character.
hints: Count the number of occupied electron shells to find the period.
Read off the number of electrons in the outermost shell to find the group.
Across Period 3, character shifts from strongly metallic (left) to non-metallic (right) as the outer-electron count rises; where does 4 outer electrons sit in that range?
guided_exercises.answer: Silicon is in **Period 3** (three occupied shells: 2, 8, 4) and **Group IV** (4 outer electrons). With 4 outer electrons, it sits roughly halfway between the metallic left side (aluminium, 3 outer electrons) and the non-metallic right side (phosphorus, 5 outer electrons) of the period, which is consistent with silicon showing some properties of both metals and non-metals (it is usually described as a metalloid at this level).
common_errors: Reading the group number from the total electron count (14) instead of the outer-shell count (4).

guided_exercises.statement: The melting points of three Group IV elements are: carbon (as diamond), extremely high; silicon, $1414\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; germanium, $938\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Using only this trend, suggest an approximate melting point for tin, the next Group IV element down, and state one reason your answer should be treated as approximate.
hints: Work out whether melting point is rising or falling as you move down the group from carbon to germanium.
Extend that direction by one more step, rather than guessing an unrelated number.
Remember that a trend gives a likely region, not a guaranteed exact figure.
guided_exercises.answer: Melting point clearly falls down this part of Group IV (extremely high, then $1414\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, then $938\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), so tin's melting point is expected to be lower still than germanium's, perhaps in the region of a few hundred degrees Celsius. This must be treated as approximate because the size of the drop is not constant between known steps, so the next drop is not guaranteed to match either previous one. (Tin's actual melting point is $232\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, inside this lower region.)
common_errors: Predicting a melting point higher than germanium's by mistakenly continuing the trend in the wrong direction.

exercises.statement: Fluorine has proton number $Z=9$ and electron configuration 2,7. State its period and group, and name one element you would expect to show similar chemistry to fluorine, giving a reason.
exercises.answer: Fluorine is in **Period 2** (two occupied shells) and **Group VII** (7 outer electrons). Chlorine (2,8,7) would be expected to show similar chemistry, because it also has exactly 7 outer-shell electrons, even though it has one more occupied shell overall.

exercises.statement: A student claims: 'Argon (2,8,8) and potassium (2,8,8,1) are basically the same, because both have 2,8,8 as part of their configuration.' Explain what is wrong with using this as a reason to put them in the same group.
exercises.answer: Group membership depends on the *outermost* shell only. Argon's outermost (third) shell holds 8 electrons and is full, while potassium has a fourth shell containing a single electron, which is its true outer shell. Although both configurations happen to contain the digits '2,8,8', that sequence is argon's complete, outermost arrangement but only part of potassium's; potassium's real outer-electron count is 1, not 8, so the two elements belong to very different groups (Group VIII and Group I) with very different chemistry.
common_errors: Treating a shared substring of the configuration as proof of shared group membership, instead of checking which shell is actually outermost for each atom.

exercises.statement: Explain, using the idea of outer-shell electrons, why a chemist can predict that rubidium (the element below potassium in Group I) will react vigorously with water, even without ever having tested rubidium directly.
exercises.answer: Rubidium sits directly below potassium in Group I, so it has the same number of outer-shell electrons (1) as every other Group I element. Because reactivity with water in this group is explained by how easily that single outer electron is lost, and the pattern of losing it increasingly easily is already established for lithium, sodium and potassium, the chemist can reasonably extend the same explanation (and expect an even more vigorous reaction) to rubidium without first testing it directly.

exercises.statement: A newly confirmed element is placed directly below caesium in Group I of the periodic table. Without looking up any further data, predict two things about this new element (one about its physical softness/reactivity, one about its likely electron configuration's outer shell), and explain your reasoning for each.
exercises.answer: Outer shell: the new element must have exactly 1 outer-shell electron, because it shares caesium's group, and group membership is defined by matching outer-electron counts regardless of how many inner shells differ. Reactivity/softness: following the general Group I trend (reactivity with water and softness generally increasing down the group, melting point generally decreasing), the new element is expected to be even softer and more reactive with water than caesium, and to have an even lower melting point — stated as a general expectation from the trend, not a guaranteed exact value, since no single pair in the group is a perfect guide to the next.

exam_questions.statement: Explain why elements in the same group of the periodic table tend to show similar chemical properties, while elements in the same period do not. Use the terms 'outer shell' and 'occupied shells' in your answer.
exam_questions.answer: Elements in the same group all have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell, and chemical behaviour is controlled mainly by what happens to those outer electrons, so elements with matching outer-shell counts tend to react in similar ways. Elements in the same period instead all have the same number of occupied shells (the same number of shells containing electrons), but their outer-shell electron counts increase steadily from left to right across the period; because it is the outer-shell count, not the number of occupied shells, that drives chemical similarity, elements across a period do not show the same chemistry as each other.
mark_scheme: States that group members share the same number of outer-shell electrons.
Links this shared outer-electron count to similar chemical behaviour down a group.
States that period members share the same number of occupied shells, not the same outer-electron count.
Explains that the outer-electron count changes across a period, which is why period members do not share chemistry.

exam_questions.statement: The melting points of three consecutive Group II elements are: magnesium, $650\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; calcium, $842\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; strontium, $777\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. A student says these data show that 'melting point always increases down Group II'. (a) State whether the student's claim is fully supported by the data, and use the values to justify your answer. **[2]** (b) Suggest a better way to describe the pattern shown by these three values. **[1]** (c) Give two reasons why a general trend can still be scientifically useful even when it is not followed by every pair of elements. **[2]**
exam_questions.answer: (a) No, the claim is not fully supported. Melting point rises from magnesium, $650\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, to calcium, $842\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, but then falls from calcium to strontium, $777\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, so it does not always increase. (b) Across these three elements melting point does not change in one consistent direction: it rises from magnesium to calcium and then falls from calcium to strontium. (c) A general trend is still useful because it allows a cautious prediction to be made for an element whose value is not given, and because an element that breaks the pattern is identified as worth investigating further.
mark_scheme: (a) States that the student's claim is not fully supported by the data.
(a) Justifies this with the values: melting point rises from 650 to $842\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Mg to Ca) but falls from 842 to $777\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Ca to Sr).
(b) Describes the pattern as not changing in one consistent direction / rising then falling, rather than as 'always increases'.
(c) One use of a general trend, e.g. it allows a cautious prediction for an element not in the data.
(c) A second, distinct use, e.g. an element that breaks the pattern is identified as worth investigating further.

challenge_questions.statement: Extended question: Explain how the concepts in Why the table has groups and periods connect to real-world applications. Use specific examples and scientific terminology in your answer.
challenge_questions.answer: A thorough answer should link why the table has groups and periods to practical applications, using correct scientific terminology and demonstrating understanding beyond the core syllabus.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
Step 1: Identify the key concepts from Why the table has groups and periods.
Step 2: Connect each concept to a real-world example.
Step 3: Use precise scientific language throughout.
Step 4: Explain the underlying principles that make these applications work.

challenge_questions.statement: Compare and contrast the following terms, explaining how they are related and how they differ: proton (atomic) number, period, group, outer (outermost) shell.
challenge_questions.answer: Students should demonstrate deep understanding by accurately distinguishing between these related concepts while showing how they connect within the topic of why the table has groups and periods.
challenge_questions.full_solution: For each term, define it precisely, then explain similarities and differences with the other terms, using examples where appropriate.

mcq.stem: What determines the strict order of elements in the modern periodic table?

options.text: Increasing relative atomic mass
options.why_wrong: mass usually increases alongside the real ordering property, but is not itself the rule used to fix the table's order.

options.text: Increasing number of electron shells
options.why_wrong: the number of shells only increases once per period, not once per element; it cannot by itself fix every element's individual position.

options.text: Increasing proton (atomic) number
Alphabetical order of the element's name
options.why_wrong: the table's order is a scientific property of the atom, not a naming convention, and element names vary by language while the table's order does not.

mcq.explanation: The periodic table is ordered by strictly increasing proton number, Z; this is the defining rule, independent of mass or naming.

mcq.stem: Silicon (2,8,4) and carbon (2,4) are both in Group IV. What do their electron configurations have in common that explains this?

options.text: They have the same total number of electrons
options.why_wrong: silicon has 14 electrons in total and carbon has 6; the totals are different.

options.text: They have the same number of occupied shells
options.why_wrong: silicon occupies three shells and carbon occupies two; the number of shells is different, which is why they are in different periods.

options.text: They are both non-metals
options.why_wrong: being a non-metal is a consequence that might follow from group position in some cases, not the defining numerical reason for shared group membership.

options.text: They have the same number of outer-shell electrons

mcq.explanation: Both atoms have exactly 4 electrons in their outermost shell, which is the defining similarity that places them in the same group.

mcq.stem: Sodium (2,8,1) and chlorine (2,8,7) are both in Period 3. Which statement correctly describes what they share?

options.text: The same number of occupied electron shells
The same number of outer-shell electrons
options.why_wrong: sodium's outer shell has 1 electron and chlorine's has 7; these are different, which is exactly why they have very different chemistry.

options.text: The same total number of electrons
options.why_wrong: sodium has 11 electrons in total and chlorine has 17; the totals are different.

options.text: The same chemical reactivity
options.why_wrong: sodium is a highly reactive metal and chlorine is a reactive non-metal; their reactivity is not the same, and reactivity is not what defines membership of the same period in any case.

mcq.explanation: Period members share the number of occupied electron shells (three, for both sodium and chlorine); their outer-electron counts, and so their chemistry, differ.

mcq.stem: A data table shows a property rising for four consecutive elements down a group, but by a different amount at each step. What is the most scientifically careful way to use this pattern to predict the value for a fifth, unlisted element further down the group?

options.text: State an exact value equal to the average of the previous step sizes added to the last known value
options.why_wrong: treating an average step size as guaranteed overstates the certainty the data actually supports, since the steps are not equal.

options.text: State that the property will probably continue to rise, giving an approximate region rather than a single exact figure
Refuse to make any prediction, since the steps are not equal
options.why_wrong: a trend can still support a cautious estimate even when its step sizes vary; refusing to use real data at all is unnecessarily cautious.

options.text: Assume the property will now fall, since four rises in a row is unlikely to continue
options.why_wrong: this reasoning has no basis in the data itself; nothing about four consistent rises makes a reversal more likely.

mcq.explanation: The careful approach uses the established direction of the trend to give an approximate region for the prediction, honestly reflecting that the exact step size is not fixed by the data.

flashcards.front: What property strictly fixes the order of elements in the periodic table?
flashcards.back: Proton (atomic) number, Z, increasing by exactly 1 between consecutive elements.

flashcards.front: What do all elements in the same group have in common?
flashcards.back: The same number of electrons in their outermost (highest) shell.

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between what a period shares and what a group shares?
flashcards.back: A period shares the same number of occupied electron shells; a group shares the same number of outer-shell electrons.

flashcards.front: Is the periodic table ordered by relative atomic mass?
flashcards.back: No. It is ordered strictly by increasing proton number; mass usually increases alongside this but is not the ordering rule itself.

flashcards.front: A data set shows a property changing by a different amount at every step down a group. How should a prediction for the next element be expressed?
flashcards.back: As an approximate region in the expected direction, not as a single guaranteed exact value.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The periodic table is ordered strictly by increasing relative atomic mass, element by element, with no exceptions.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Early historical tables (such as Mendeleev's) were built mainly around atomic mass, and mass does increase alongside proton number for almost every element, so the two orderings look identical unless a learner checks closely.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner justifies an element's position by quoting or estimating its atomic mass rather than its proton number, or is puzzled by any case where mass order and proton-number order do not obviously match.
misconceptions.correct_model: The modern periodic table is ordered strictly by increasing proton (atomic) number, Z. Relative atomic mass usually increases alongside Z, but Z, not mass, is the actual ordering rule.
misconceptions.remediation: Point out that proton number increases by exactly 1 between every pair of consecutive elements with no exceptions anywhere in the table, then show that this is the rule that actually fixes the order, independent of mass.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Elements in the same period (the same row) must have the same number of outer-shell electrons, in the same way that elements in the same group do.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners over-generalise the useful 'same group means same outer-electron count' rule to the other axis of the table, assuming any shared row or column works the same way.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner claims that sodium and chlorine (both Period 3) have the same number of outer electrons, or expects every Period 3 element to react in a similar way.
misconceptions.correct_model: Elements in the same period share the same number of occupied electron shells, not the same number of outer electrons; the outer-shell electron count instead increases steadily from left to right across the period, which is exactly what changes the elements' character from metallic to non-metallic.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare sodium (2,8,1) and chlorine (2,8,7) side by side: the same number of shells (3) but very different outer-electron counts (1 versus 7), and very different chemistry.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A trend identified down a group (for example, 'melting point decreases') must hold exactly for every single neighbouring pair of elements, with no exceptions allowed.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Classroom trends are often stated as a single confident sentence ('reactivity increases down the group'), and a learner reads the word 'trend' as meaning 'law without exceptions'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner rejects, or becomes confused by, real data that shows the overall pattern holding but one specific adjacent pair breaking it.
misconceptions.correct_model: A 'general trend' describes the overall direction of change across a group; it can still contain individual exceptions. A prediction made from a trend is a cautious estimate of a likely region, never a guaranteed exact value.
misconceptions.remediation: Show a real data set where the overall direction holds but one neighbouring pair breaks it, and ask the learner to redescribe the trend using words that allow for that exception, such as 'generally decreases'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining an element's position using its relative atomic mass instead of its proton number.
common_mistakes.why: Mass and proton number increase together for almost every element, so the difference is easy to miss without checking closely.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always state the ordering rule as 'increasing proton number', and treat mass as a separate, usually-but-not-always-matching property.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting elements in the same period to share chemistry the way elements in the same group do.
common_mistakes.why: Learners generalise the useful group rule onto the other axis of the table without checking what a period actually guarantees.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask separately: 'how many shells are occupied?' for period membership, and 'how many electrons are in the outer shell?' for group membership.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a general group trend as an exact rule with no possible exceptions.
common_mistakes.why: Trends are often taught as a single confident sentence, which reads as an absolute law.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State trends as 'generally' increasing or decreasing, and treat any prediction made from them as an approximate region, not an exact figure.

exam_notes: When explaining group similarity or period change, always name the specific electron feature involved (outer-shell count for groups, occupied-shell count for periods) rather than simply saying 'the electron structure is similar/different'.

When asked to predict a value from a trend, state the direction and an approximate region, and explicitly note that the prediction is not exact, to access marks for scientific caution as well as for the direction itself.

Proton number and group/period position should be read directly from a supplied configuration or data table in the exam, not recalled from memory, unless the specific element is one of the very common ones (H, O, C, Na, Cl) covered throughout the course.

summary.big_idea: The periodic table is ordered strictly by increasing proton number; its groups collect elements that share an outer-electron count, and its periods collect elements that share a number of occupied shells, which is why groups predict chemistry and periods do not.
key_points: Elements are placed in order of strictly increasing proton number, Z, not relative atomic mass.
Group members share the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why they show similar chemistry.
Period members share the same number of occupied shells; their outer-electron count instead increases across the row, so periods do not share chemistry.
A trend down a group describes a general direction and supports a cautious, approximate prediction, not an exact guaranteed value.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Same group means same outer-shell electron count; that single number, not the total number of electrons, is what predicts shared chemistry.

exit_check.question: Caesium (Group I) has the configuration 2,8,18,18,8,1. Without looking anything up, state its outer-shell electron count and one physical/chemical property you would expect it to show, with a reason.
exit_check.answer: Caesium's outer shell holds 1 electron, matching every other Group I element. It is expected to react very vigorously with water (even more so than potassium), because reactivity with water increases down Group I as that single outer electron becomes easier to lose from an atom with more inner shells shielding it.

theory_blocks.title: Metals that float and fizz
theory_blocks.body:
Drop a small piece of sodium into a trough of water and it skates across the surface, fizzing and sometimes bursting into a yellow-orange flame, before disappearing into a colourless solution that turns universal indicator deep purple.

Lithium does the same thing more gently; potassium does it more violently, often igniting immediately with a lilac flame.

All three metals are soft enough to cut with a knife, and all three are so much less dense than typical metals that lithium, sodium and (just) potassium actually float on water, at least until they react away.

These are the alkali metals, Group I. Their shared behaviour is not a coincidence: every member has [[blue:exactly one electron in its outer shell]],

and the pattern of how easily that one electron is lost changes in a regular way as you move down the group.

theory_blocks.title: Three properties, three separate trends
theory_blocks.body:
The table below gives verified data for the first three alkali metals.

| Element | Proton number, $Z$ | Melting point ($^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) | Density ($\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lithium, Li | 3 | 181 | 0.53 |
| Sodium, Na | 11 | 98 | 0.97 |
| Potassium, K | 19 | 63 | 0.86 |

Reading down each column separately:

- **Melting point generally decreases** down the group: $181 \rightarrow 98 \rightarrow 63\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, a clean, consistent fall at every step.
- **Density does not rise smoothly at every step**: it rises from lithium to sodium ($0.53 \rightarrow 0.97$) but then *falls* from sodium to potassium ($0.97 \rightarrow 0.86$), even though the overall pattern across the group (and continuing to rubidium, $1.53\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) is upward.
- **Reactivity with water generally increases** down the group: lithium reacts steadily, sodium more vigorously, potassium violently enough to ignite its own hydrogen.

The figure below sets the first two of these properties (melting point and density) side by side, reading down the group from top to bottom.

assets.caption: Melting point and density of lithium, sodium and potassium, drawn to scale down Group I. The melting-point bars shrink steadily at every step; the density bars grow overall but sodium is actually denser than potassium directly below it, a genuine local exception inside the general upward trend.
assets.purpose: Shows two real property trends to scale from the same three elements, so a learner can see directly that melting point falls cleanly while density rises only in general, not at every single step.

theory_blocks.title: What the reaction with water makes
theory_blocks.body:
Every Group I metal reacts with cold water in the same way, and the reaction always makes the same two products: a [[blue:metal hydroxide]], which dissolves to give an alkaline solution, and [[blue:hydrogen gas]].

General word equation:

alkali metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen

For the three metals named in the syllabus:

- lithium + water → lithium hydroxide + hydrogen, $2\mathrm{Li(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{LiOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$
- sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen, $2\mathrm{Na(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$
- potassium + water → potassium hydroxide + hydrogen, $2\mathrm{K(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$

Each one needs two atoms of metal and two molecules of water for every molecule of hydrogen.

A common slip is to write $\mathrm{Na} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{H_2}$, which leaves three hydrogen atoms on the right but only two on the left.

**What you would see**

- The metal floats, because all three are less dense than water, and moves about the surface.
- Bubbles of gas are given off, so the reaction fizzes. Sodium and potassium melt into a shiny ball, because the reaction releases enough heat; potassium's hydrogen normally ignites, burning with a lilac flame.
- The piece of metal gets smaller and disappears, leaving a colourless solution.

**How the two products are tested**

- *The gas:* collect it in a test tube and hold a lighted splint at the mouth — hydrogen burns with a squeaky 'pop'.
- *The solution:* add universal indicator, which turns purple, or dip red litmus paper, which turns blue. Both show that the solution is alkaline, because the metal hydroxide formed is an alkali.

assets.caption: Sodium reacting with cold water: the metal floats and moves about the surface, hydrogen bubbles off and the sodium hydroxide formed turns universal indicator purple. The two products are identified by the squeaky-pop test for hydrogen and by the indicator.
assets.purpose: Ties each observable feature of the reaction to the product it identifies, so the word and symbol equations are read as a description of something seen rather than as a formula to memorise.

theory_blocks.title: Reactivity with water: a teacher demonstration, never a student experiment
theory_blocks.body:
The Group I water reaction becomes genuinely hazardous very quickly: potassium's reaction is violent enough to spit molten metal and ignite its hydrogen, so it is only ever shown by a teacher, using a tiny piece behind a safety screen (rubidium and caesium are far too dangerous to show at all).

What a student is expected to know is the description and trend of the reaction (fizzing, moving across the surface, an alkaline solution forming, increasing vigour down the group), evidenced by data and verified descriptions, not by personally testing every element.

[[blue:Treat 'describe the reaction' and 'carry out the reaction' as entirely separate skills]]: this course asks only for the first.

theory_blocks.title: Predicting one property at a time
theory_blocks.body:
To predict a property of an unlisted Group I element (for example rubidium, directly below potassium) from supplied data:

1. **Choose one property at a time.** Never assume that because one property increases, another must increase too; each property has its own column and its own trend.
2. **Check the step sizes for that property specifically.** If they are roughly consistent (as with melting point above), a prediction can be reasonably precise. If they are not consistent (as with density above), state a wider, more cautious region instead.
3. **Give the prediction as a reasoned estimate**, naming the direction and, where justified, an approximate size, rather than a single confidently exact number pulled from nowhere.

This is the Supplement skill this unit keeps returning to: using real, supplied data honestly, rather than either refusing to predict or over-stating the precision the data can support.

keywords.definition: An element of Group I of the periodic table (lithium, sodium, potassium and others below them); soft, low-density, reactive metals with one outer-shell electron.
The overall direction of change of a property across a group, which may still contain individual exceptions at particular steps.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid; decreases steadily down Group I.
Mass per unit volume; generally increases down Group I, though not at every individual step between neighbouring elements.
How vigorously an element reacts when added to water; generally increases down Group I, from gentle fizzing (lithium) to a violent, often igniting reaction (potassium and below).

worked_examples.statement: **Reading the table.** Using the melting-point data for lithium (181 °C), sodium (98 °C) and potassium (63 °C), state which Group I metal has the highest melting point and which has the lowest, and describe the trend in one sentence.
solution: Lithium has the highest melting point (181 °C) and potassium has the lowest (63 °C) among these three.
Melting point decreases steadily down the group: lithium, then sodium, then potassium, each lower than the one above.
worked_examples.interpretation: A simple, clean read-off establishes that 'down the group' has a consistent physical meaning (lower melting point) before the density data complicates the picture.

worked_examples.statement: **The density exception.** A student looks at the density data (Li 0.53, Na 0.97, K 0.86 g/cm³) and says, 'this can't be right, density has to increase every step down a group.' Explain why the student is mistaken, without dismissing the general trend entirely.
solution: The data is correct: sodium (0.97 g/cm³) really is denser than potassium (0.86 g/cm³) directly below it.

A 'general trend' describes the overall pattern, not a guarantee for every single neighbouring pair; the overall direction from lithium through to heavier alkali metals such as rubidium (1.53 g/cm³) is still upward.
The student's error is treating 'general trend' as meaning 'exact rule with no exceptions', rather than as a dominant pattern that can still contain a genuine local exception.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming a documented exception means the data must be wrong, instead of revising the description of the trend.

worked_examples.statement: **Predicting rubidium's melting point.** Using the melting points of lithium (181 °C), sodium (98 °C) and potassium (63 °C), predict an approximate melting point for rubidium, the next Group I element down, and justify your reasoning.
solution: Find the step sizes: Li to Na falls by 83 °C (181 to 98); Na to K falls by 35 °C (98 to 63).
The falls are both substantial but shrinking, so a reasonable next fall is smaller again than 35 °C, perhaps in the region of 15-30 °C.
Starting from potassium's 63 °C and subtracting a fall in that region gives an estimated range of roughly 33-48 °C for rubidium.

This is stated as a region, not an exact figure, because the step sizes are shrinking rather than staying constant, so the next step size is not fixed by the data alone. (Rubidium's actual melting point is 39 °C, inside this estimated region.)
worked_examples.interpretation: This models exactly the Supplement skill required: using consistent-direction, shrinking-step data to build a defensible region rather than a false-precision single value.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Subtracting the most recent step size (35 °C) unchanged, ignoring that the steps themselves are shrinking, which would under-shoot the prediction.

guided_exercises.statement: A data table shows that sodium reacts with water fast enough to move rapidly across the surface and occasionally catch fire, while lithium reacts more gently, fizzing steadily without catching fire. Predict, with a reason, how you would expect potassium's reaction with water to compare to sodium's.
hints: Identify the direction of the reactivity trend shown by lithium and sodium so far.
Potassium sits directly below sodium in the group.
State your prediction as a comparison (more/less vigorous than sodium), not as a made-up exact description.
guided_exercises.answer: Reactivity with water increases down Group I (lithium gentlest, sodium more vigorous). Since potassium sits directly below sodium, it is expected to react even more vigorously than sodium: more violently, more likely to ignite immediately, and faster overall. (In reality, potassium's reaction is so violent that it is only shown by a teacher, using a tiny piece behind a safety screen.)
common_errors: Predicting that potassium's reaction will be similar in vigour to sodium's, rather than extending the established increasing trend one step further.

guided_exercises.statement: Caesium is a Group I element below rubidium. Rubidium's melting point is 39 °C and caesium's is 28 °C. A student is asked to predict francium's melting point (the next element down) and answers 'about 28 °C, the same as caesium's value.' Evaluate this prediction and suggest an improvement.
hints: Work out the size of the fall from rubidium to caesium (39 to 28 °C).
A melting point equal to caesium's value is no fall at all; compare that to the actual step size just calculated.
A reasonable prediction should continue a fall of a broadly similar or slightly smaller size, expressed as a region.
guided_exercises.answer: The fall from rubidium to caesium is 11 °C (39 to 28), so a prediction of 'about 28 °C' (no fall at all) ignores the established pattern: melting point has fallen at every step down Group I. A better estimate continues a fall of a similar or slightly smaller size than 11 °C (the falls have been shrinking down the group), giving an approximate region of roughly 17-23 °C rather than a value equal to caesium's own melting point. (Francium is so intensely radioactive that its melting point has never been measured reliably and quoted estimates vary; the key skill here is the reasoning about step size, not an exact figure.)
common_errors: Picking a value close to the last known value without actually calculating and continuing the established step size.

exercises.statement: State two physical properties that lithium, sodium and potassium have in common (not necessarily identical values, but a shared general description), and one property for which their values clearly differ from each other.
exercises.answer: Shared general description: all three are soft metals that can be cut with a knife, and all three are much less dense than typical metals (dense enough to float, or nearly float, on water). Property that clearly differs: melting point (181 °C for lithium, 98 °C for sodium, 63 °C for potassium are all markedly different from one another).

exercises.statement: Explain why it would be incorrect to say 'every property of the Group I metals increases down the group', using the melting-point data (Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C) as your evidence.
exercises.answer: Melting point is a clear counter-example: it decreases steadily down the group (181, then 98, then 63 °C), rather than increasing. This shows that 'down the group' does not mean 'every property increases'; each property must be checked individually, since some (melting point) decrease while others (reactivity with water, generally density) increase.
common_errors: Trying to defend the claim by only discussing reactivity or density, while ignoring the melting-point data that directly contradicts it.

exercises.statement: Using the density data (Li 0.53, Na 0.97, K 0.86 g/cm³), describe the overall trend in density down Group I in a way that remains accurate even though density does not rise at every single step.
exercises.answer: Density generally increases down Group I overall (lithium is the least dense, and density continues to rise further down the group, for example rubidium at 1.53 g/cm³), but the rise is not perfectly consistent at every step: sodium (0.97) is actually slightly denser than potassium (0.86) immediately below it. A fair description is 'density generally increases down the group, though not at every individual step.'

exercises.statement: Caesium is the Group I metal two places below potassium (potassium, then rubidium, then caesium). Using only the data already given in this lesson — densities Li 0.53, Na 0.97, K 0.86 g/cm³ and Rb 1.53 g/cm³, and the described reactivity of lithium, sodium and potassium with water — predict, with reasoning, (a) how caesium's density compares with potassium's, and (b) how vigorously caesium would react with water compared with potassium. For each prediction, say how confident you can be and why.
exercises.answer: (a) Density: the overall direction down Group I is upward — 0.53 for lithium, then 0.97 for sodium, and 1.53 for rubidium below potassium — so caesium, one place below rubidium, is predicted to be denser than potassium's 0.86 g/cm³ and probably denser than rubidium's 1.53 g/cm³ as well. This prediction should be given as a direction and a wide region rather than a figure, because the density data contains a real local exception (sodium 0.97 is denser than potassium 0.86), so the step sizes are not a reliable guide. (Caesium's actual density is 1.93 g/cm³.) (b) Reactivity with water: reactivity increases at every step described in this lesson (lithium fizzes steadily, sodium is more vigorous and may ignite, potassium ignites immediately), with no exception, so caesium is predicted to react even more violently than potassium — fast enough to be explosive. This prediction can be made with more confidence than the density one, because the reactivity trend is consistent at every step, whereas the density trend is not.

exercises.statement: Potassium reacts with cold water in the same way as sodium. Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation (with state symbols) for this reaction, and state one observation that shows potassium's reaction is more vigorous than sodium's.
exercises.answer: Word equation: potassium + water → potassium hydroxide + hydrogen. Symbol equation: $2\mathrm{K(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$. Observation: the hydrogen given off ignites straight away and burns with a lilac flame, whereas sodium often reacts without catching fire.
common_errors: Writing K + H2O → KOH + H2 without balancing, which leaves three hydrogen atoms on the right and only two on the left.

exam_questions.statement: The melting points of lithium, sodium and potassium are 181 °C, 98 °C and 63 °C respectively. (a) Describe the trend in melting point down Group I. (b) Predict an approximate melting point for rubidium, the next element down, showing your reasoning.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Melting point decreases steadily down Group I: each element has a clearly lower melting point than the one above it (181, then 98, then 63 °C). (b) The fall from lithium to sodium is 83 °C, and from sodium to potassium is 35 °C; the size of the fall is shrinking, so a reasonable next fall is smaller again, perhaps 15-30 °C, giving an estimated melting point for rubidium of approximately 33-48 °C (lower than potassium's 63 °C, but by a smaller step than the previous falls).
mark_scheme: (a) States that melting point decreases down the group, citing at least two of the given values correctly.
(a) Describes the trend as consistent/clear across all three given values.
(b) Calculates or clearly uses the shrinking step sizes (83 °C, then 35 °C) to justify the direction and approximate size of the next step.
(b) Gives a sensible approximate value or region for rubidium's melting point, lower than potassium's 63 °C, rather than an unjustified exact figure.

exam_questions.statement: Densities of lithium, sodium and potassium are 0.53, 0.97 and 0.86 g/cm³ respectively. A textbook states, 'density generally increases down Group I.' Using the given data, (a) explain whether this statement is consistent with all three values, (b) explain why the statement can still be considered a correct description of the overall trend, and (c) state what a scientist should do differently when using this trend to predict rubidium's density, compared with using the melting-point trend from the same group.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Not fully consistent at every step: density rises from lithium to sodium (0.53 to 0.97) but falls from sodium to potassium (0.97 to 0.86), so the increase is not seen at every individual step. (b) The statement can still be considered correct as a description of the overall, general pattern: density is clearly higher by the time you reach heavier Group I elements such as rubidium (1.53 g/cm³) than it is at lithium, even though one local step (sodium to potassium) goes against the general direction; a 'general trend' is explicitly allowed to contain such exceptions. (c) Because the density data is not consistently increasing at every step (unlike the cleanly, consistently falling melting-point data), a scientist should predict rubidium's density with a wider, more cautious region and should not rely on the most recent step size (sodium to potassium, which actually fell) as a reliable guide to the next step; the melting-point trend, being far more internally consistent, supports a tighter, more confident predicted region by comparison.
mark_scheme: (a) Identifies that the data falls from Na to K, so does not increase at every step.
(a) Uses the specific numerical data (0.53, 0.97, 0.86) correctly.
(b) Explains that an overall/general trend can remain correct despite a local exception, with reference to the wider pattern (e.g. rubidium).
(c) States that the prediction should be made more cautiously / with a wider region because of the inconsistent step sizes.
(c) Correctly contrasts this with the melting-point data's more consistent, shrinking-but-same-direction step sizes.

exam_questions.statement: A small piece of sodium is added to a trough of cold water containing a few drops of universal indicator. The sodium floats, fizzes and moves about the surface until it disappears. (a) Name the two products of the reaction. **[1]** (b) Write a word equation for the reaction. **[1]** (c) Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction, including state symbols. **[2]** (d) Describe a test that would show the gas given off is hydrogen, and give the result. **[2]** (e) The universal indicator turns purple. State what this tells you about the solution formed. **[1]**
exam_questions.answer: (a) Sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. (b) Sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen. (c) $2\mathrm{Na(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$. (d) Collect the gas in a test tube and hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube; hydrogen burns with a squeaky 'pop'. (e) The solution is alkaline: it contains sodium hydroxide, so its pH is above 7.
mark_scheme: (a) Names both products: sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.
(b) Word equation correct: sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen.
(c) Correct formulae for all four species: Na, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, NaOH and $\mathrm{H_2}$.
(c) Equation correctly balanced with state symbols: $2\mathrm{Na(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$.
(d) Collects the gas and applies a lighted splint to it.
(d) States the result: the gas burns with a squeaky 'pop'.
(e) States that the solution is alkaline (accept pH above 7, or contains an alkali / sodium hydroxide).

challenge_questions.answer: A thorough answer should link group i: properties and prediction to practical applications, using correct scientific terminology and demonstrating understanding beyond the core syllabus.

challenge_questions.statement: Compare and contrast the following terms, explaining how they are related and how they differ: alkali metal, general trend, melting point, density.
challenge_questions.answer: Students should demonstrate deep understanding by accurately distinguishing between these related concepts while showing how they connect within the topic of group i: properties and prediction.
challenge_questions.full_solution: For each term, define it precisely, then explain similarities and differences with the other terms, using examples where appropriate.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly describes the trend in melting point down Group I, using the data Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C?

options.text: Melting point increases steadily down the group
options.why_wrong: the data falls at every step (181, 98, 63 °C), the opposite of increasing.

options.text: Melting point stays roughly constant down the group
options.why_wrong: the values change substantially (by 83 °C and then 35 °C), far from constant.

options.text: Melting point decreases steadily down the group
Melting point has no clear pattern down the group
options.why_wrong: all three given values fall in the same direction at every step, which is a clear, consistent pattern.

mcq.explanation: Each value is lower than the one above it (181, then 98, then 63 °C), giving a clear, consistent decreasing trend.

mcq.stem: Sodium's density (0.97 g/cm³) is higher than potassium's (0.86 g/cm³), even though density generally increases down Group I. What is the best way to describe this?

options.text: The data must be wrong, since density always increases down a group
options.why_wrong: the data is correct and well documented; 'always' is not what a general trend guarantees.

options.text: Density does not really follow a trend down Group I at all
options.why_wrong: the overall direction is still upward across the group (continuing to higher values further down), so there is a real general trend, just not a perfectly consistent one.

options.text: Sodium should not really be classed as a Group I element because of this
options.why_wrong: group membership depends on outer-shell electron count, not on perfectly following every physical-property trend; sodium is unambiguously Group I.

options.text: This is a genuine local exception inside an overall general trend

mcq.explanation: A general trend describes the overall pattern and can still contain a genuine local exception, exactly as seen here between sodium and potassium.

mcq.stem: Which property of Group I metals increases down the group, alongside reactivity with water?

options.text: Density, generally
Melting point
options.why_wrong: melting point decreases down the group (181, 98, 63 °C for Li, Na, K), the opposite direction to reactivity.

options.text: Hardness
options.why_wrong: the Group I metals generally become softer, not harder, down the group, not a property emphasised as increasing here.

options.text: Electron shell count only
options.why_wrong: while the number of shells does increase down the group, this is a structural fact used to explain the trends, not itself the kind of measured physical property being compared here.

mcq.explanation: Density generally increases down Group I (0.53, 0.97, 0.86, then 1.53 g/cm³ for Li, Na, K, Rb), even though one local step is an exception, in the same general direction as reactivity with water.

mcq.stem: A learner is asked to predict rubidium's melting point from Li (181 °C), Na (98 °C) and K (63 °C), and answers 'exactly 28 °C, because I looked it up once.' What is the main problem with this answer, as a response to a prediction task?

options.text: 28 °C is numerically impossible for a Group I metal
options.why_wrong: 28 °C is not an unreasonable value in itself; the objection is about method, not about this specific number being physically impossible.

options.text: The answer does not show reasoning from the supplied data, which is what a prediction task is assessing
Melting point cannot be predicted at all for Group I elements
options.why_wrong: the worked examples in this lesson show that a reasoned approximate prediction is both possible and exactly what is required.

options.text: The answer should have used the density data instead of the melting-point data
options.why_wrong: the question specifically asks for melting point, so melting-point data is the correct data set to reason from.

mcq.explanation: A prediction task assesses reasoning from the supplied step sizes and direction, not recall of a memorised figure with no shown working, however numerically close that figure might happen to be.

flashcards.front: Name the first three Group I (alkali) metals, in order down the group.
flashcards.back: Lithium, sodium, potassium.

flashcards.front: How does melting point change down Group I?
flashcards.back: It generally decreases: lithium 181 °C, sodium 98 °C, potassium 63 °C.

flashcards.front: Do melting point and reactivity with water change in the same direction down Group I?
flashcards.back: No: melting point generally decreases down the group, while reactivity with water generally increases.

flashcards.front: Does density increase at every single step down Group I?
flashcards.back: No. It generally increases overall, but sodium (0.97 g/cm³) is actually denser than potassium (0.86 g/cm³) directly below it — a real local exception inside the general trend.

flashcards.front: How should you state a predicted value for an unlisted Group I element's property?
flashcards.back: As an approximate region built from the direction and step sizes of the supplied data, not as a memorised or guessed exact figure.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Every physical and chemical property of the Group I metals increases as you go down the group, with no exceptions.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Reactivity with water and softness both increase down the group; a learner who notices two properties both increasing over-generalises to 'everything increases'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner assumes density must also increase smoothly at every step, or is surprised that melting point decreases rather than increases down the group.
misconceptions.correct_model: Different properties follow their own trends: melting point generally decreases down Group I, while reactivity with water and (usually) density generally increase; each property must be checked on its own data, not assumed to follow the same direction as any other.
misconceptions.remediation: Put melting point, density and reactivity data for lithium, sodium and potassium side by side and ask the learner to describe the direction of each column separately before drawing any general conclusion.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Because density generally increases down Group I, every individual neighbouring pair of elements must show a higher density than the one above it, with no exceptions.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The general statement 'density increases down the group' is taught as a short, confident rule, and learners read a general rule as applying exactly to every single pair rather than to the overall pattern.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner refuses to accept, or tries to explain away, real data showing sodium with a higher density than potassium directly below it.
misconceptions.correct_model: Sodium (about 0.97 g/cm³) is in fact slightly denser than potassium (about 0.86 g/cm³) directly below it, even though the overall pattern down the group, taken as a whole, is for density to increase; this is a genuine, well-documented local exception inside a real overall trend, exactly the kind of case a 'general trend' is meant to allow for.
misconceptions.remediation: Show the actual three-element density data (Li 0.53, Na 0.97, K 0.86 g/cm³) and ask the learner to describe the overall pattern in words that remain true even though the middle step breaks the simple 'always increases' version.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Making a correct prediction about an unlisted Group I element's property requires already knowing (recalling) its exact measured value.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners are used to exam questions that reward a recalled exact number, so they assume a 'predict' question is secretly a 'remember' question in disguise.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner refuses to attempt a prediction without being given the exact figure first, or treats an estimated region as an unsatisfying, incomplete answer.
misconceptions.correct_model: A prediction task asks for a reasoned, approximate value or region built from the direction and (where relevant) the size of the trend in the supplied data, not a memorised exact figure; a well-reasoned estimate that falls in the right region, with working shown, earns full credit.
misconceptions.remediation: Practise stating predictions explicitly as a region ('somewhere lower than X, probably around Y') rather than a single number, and confirm that this is the form the skill actually requires.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming every Group I property changes in the same direction down the group.
common_mistakes.why: Reactivity and (generally) density both increase, so it feels natural to expect melting point to increase too.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check each property's own data column separately before stating its trend; melting point in particular decreases down the group.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the sodium/potassium density exception as a sign that the data or the trend is wrong.
common_mistakes.why: A 'general trend' is often taught as a short absolute rule, so any exception feels like a contradiction rather than an expected feature.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Describe trends as 'generally' increasing or decreasing, and treat a single documented local exception as compatible with, not a refutation of, the overall pattern.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving a single precise predicted value with no reasoning shown, instead of a justified approximate region.
common_mistakes.why: Learners are used to 'predict' questions secretly wanting a memorised exact answer.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always show the step-size calculation from the supplied data and express the final answer as a reasoned region or direction.

exam_notes: When describing a Group I trend, name the specific property (melting point, density, reactivity with water) rather than saying 'the properties change'; different properties change in different, sometimes opposite, directions.

When data shows an exception to an otherwise clear trend, describe the general pattern accurately ('generally increases') rather than either denying the exception or abandoning the whole idea of a trend.
A numerical prediction question is marked mainly on reasoning from the supplied data (step sizes, direction), so always show that working rather than writing only a final number.

summary.big_idea: Group I metals share a family of behaviours because they share one outer electron, but each individual physical property (melting point, density, reactivity) follows its own trend down the group, and a real trend can still include a local exception.
key_points: Lithium, sodium and potassium are soft, low-density, reactive metals that fizz or ignite in water, with vigour increasing down the group.
Melting point decreases steadily down Group I: 181 °C, 98 °C, 63 °C for lithium, sodium, potassium.
Density generally increases down the group but sodium (0.97 g/cm³) is actually denser than potassium (0.86 g/cm³) directly below it — a genuine local exception.
A prediction for an unlisted element should be built from the direction and step sizes of supplied data and given as an approximate region, never as a memorised exact figure.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Each Group I property has its own trend — melting point falls, reactivity rises, density rises overall but not at every step — so check the data for the specific property being asked about.

exit_check.question: Potassium's melting point is 63 °C and rubidium's is 39 °C. Predict, with reasoning, an approximate melting point for caesium, the next element down.
exit_check.answer: The fall from potassium to rubidium is 24 °C (63 to 39). Down Group I the falls have been shrinking (83, then 35, then 24 °C from lithium onwards), so the next fall is likely to be smaller again, perhaps about 10-20 °C, giving an estimated region of roughly 19-29 °C for caesium. (Caesium's actual melting point is 28 °C, inside this region; the key is the reasoned estimate, not an exact match.)

theory_blocks.title: Three very different-looking elements, one family
theory_blocks.body:
Open a jar of chlorine and you would meet a pale yellow-green gas with a sharp, choking smell. Open a sealed tube of bromine and a deep red-brown liquid sits there, giving off an orange vapour the moment the lid comes off.

Iodine looks nothing like either: a dark grey-black solid that, gently warmed, skips the liquid stage entirely and turns straight into a striking purple vapour.

Three completely different physical appearances, from gas to liquid to solid at room temperature — yet all three are placed in the same group, Group VII, the halogens.

What unites them is the same kind of pattern seen in Group I: each halogen atom has [[blue:7 electrons in its outer shell]], one short of the stable, full 8 that a noble gas has.

That shared 'one electron short' structure is what makes every halogen reactive in a similar way, while the size of the atom (and so its physical state and density) changes steadily down the group.

theory_blocks.title: State, appearance and two opposite trends
theory_blocks.body:
Chlorine, bromine and iodine are non-metals made of **diatomic** molecules (two atoms bonded together: Cl$_2$, Br$_2$, I$_2$). At room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.):

| Halogen | State at r.t.p. | Colour | Boiling/melting point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chlorine, Cl$_2$ | gas | pale yellow-green | b.p. $-34\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ |
| Bromine, Br$_2$ | liquid | red-brown | b.p. $59\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ |
| Iodine, I$_2$ | solid | grey-black (purple vapour on gentle heating) | m.p. $114\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ |

Two trends run down the group in **opposite directions**:

- **Density generally increases** down the group: chlorine is the least dense, iodine the densest. Alongside this, the state changes from gas to liquid to solid, because the molecules get larger going down the group and attract each other more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them.
- **Reactivity generally decreases** down the group: chlorine reacts the most readily, iodine the least. This happens because each halogen's reactivity depends on how strongly it attracts one extra electron to complete its outer shell, and that attraction weakens as the outer shell sits further from the nucleus in the larger atoms lower down the group.

The figure below sets state, appearance and these verified temperatures side by side.
